clue.text: Team whose success was recorded by Aurelian Townshend?

definitions.text: Team whose success was recorded by Aurelian Townshend?

parts.words: Team whose success was recorded by Aurelian Townshend?
parts.note: Townshend wrote a 1632 court masque celebrating the triumph of an old poetic name for Britain, which is also part of a football team's name (West Bromwich)

explanation.surface: A question about which sports side had its victory chronicled by a Caroline poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Aurelian Townshend's masque is titled after the triumph of this ancient name for Britain; 'Team' points to West Bromwich's football club, which carries the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient poetic name for Britain is both the subject of Townshend's masque and the second word of a famous English football club.

clue.text: One of her suitors sustained slender hopes

definitions.text: One of her suitors sustained slender hopes

parts.words: One of her suitors sustained slender hopes
parts.note: in The Merry Wives of Windsor her suitors include Master Slender, so 'slender hopes' are literally his

explanation.surface: A woman one of whose admirers had little chance of success.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Merry Wives of Windsor, Page's daughter is courted by Slender, Dr Caius and Fenton; 'slender' looks like 'faint' but names the suitor.
explanation.definitionFit: Page's daughter in The Merry Wives of Windsor is wooed by Slender and finally marries Fenton.

clue.text: "ed Sarah, and I/. Is that thing alive?" (John Berryman)

definitions.text: "ed Sarah, and I/. Is that thing alive?" (John Berryman)

parts.words: "ed Sarah, and I/. Is that thing alive?" (John Berryman)
parts.note: a quotation with its gaps lost in printing: the word fills the blank before 'ed' and the blank after the line break

explanation.surface: A line from Berryman's Homage to Mistress Bradstreet, on childbirth.
explanation.walkthrough: The blanks were lost in printing: the line runs '___ed Sarah, and I / ___. Is that thing alive?', the speaker flowering as her child is born.
explanation.definitionFit: Berryman's verb for flowering or flourishing completes both gaps in the stanza on Anne Bradstreet giving birth.

clue.text: Peculiar relations, like the owners of The Moonstone

indicators.note: peculiar means odd, so the letters of relations are rearranged into a new word

explanation.surface: Odd family members resembling the guardians of a stolen gem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peculiar' rearranges RELATIONS. In Wilkie Collins's The Moonstone, the diamond belongs to Hindu priests who pursue it to England.
explanation.definitionFit: In Collins's novel the sacred diamond rightfully belongs to three Brahmin guardians from India, called Easterners.

clue.text: A mother to a Jarrow scholar was a carpenter

parts.note: a dam is the mother of an animal, especially a horse
the Venerable Bede was the monk-historian of the monastery at Jarrow in north-east England

explanation.surface: A family history claiming a monk's mother worked in carpentry.
explanation.walkthrough: George Eliot's title hero is a village carpenter; the Venerable Bede wrote his histories at Jarrow, in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's title character works as a carpenter and joiner in rural Hayslope.

clue.text: Italian noblewoman, as defined in Webster (7, 2, )

definitions.text: Italian noblewoman, as defined in Webster

parts.words: Italian noblewoman, as defined in Webster
parts.note: Webster suggests the dictionary but is John Webster, whose Jacobean tragedy is named after its heroine's title

explanation.surface: Looking up an aristocrat's definition in a dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: Webster looks like the American dictionary, but it is the Jacobean dramatist John Webster.
explanation.definitionFit: John Webster's revenge tragedy is named for its heroine, a widowed noblewoman of Amalfi.

clue.text: He initiates many innocent light novel editions

indicators.note: to initiate is to begin, so each word that follows gives its beginning letter

explanation.surface: An author whose gentle books launched many lighthearted editions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initiates' takes the first letters of 'many innocent light novel editions'; A. A. Milne wrote gentle comic novels as well as Winnie-the-Pooh.
explanation.definitionFit: He stands for a man; A. A. Milne, the man meant, wrote light comic fiction such as The Red House Mystery.

clue.text: Only half as significant as the Quarto?

definitions.text: Only half as significant as the Quarto?

parts.words: Only half as significant as the Quarto?
parts.note: a book size whose sheets are folded into eight leaves, so its pages are half the size of a quarto's four

explanation.surface: Questioning whether a text matters only half as much as Shakespeare's Quartos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'significant' here means large: folding a sheet three times gives eight leaves, each half a quarto leaf.
explanation.definitionFit: Octavo, also written 8vo and spelt out this way, is the book format with eight leaves to a sheet.

clue.text: Additional charges for very minor characters

definitions.meaning: items billed on top of the basic price
walk-on performers in a film or play with no lines

explanation.surface: Being billed more for hiring walk-on actors.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both surcharges added to a bill and background performers hired for crowd scenes.

clue.text: Matchless Congreve character

parts.note: 'matchless' seems to mean peerless but means without a match in marriage, the title figure of Congreve's first comedy

explanation.surface: Praise for an unrivalled figure in Restoration comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Matchless' suggests unequalled but means unmarried: Congreve's 1693 comedy is named after its long-unwed title figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Congreve's first comedy, of 1693, is named for Heartwell, a surly unmarried man.

clue.text: Stone Age north-eastern circle illuminated this Latin

parts.note: NE is the standard abbreviation for north-east
a circle is the shape of the letter O
lit means lighted up
hic is the Latin word for 'this'

explanation.surface: Something about lighting up a prehistoric stone circle in Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: The later Stone Age, when polished stone tools and farming appeared, is the period this adjective describes.

clue.text: Terry Pratchett's sort of fantastic ()

parts.note: the second Discworld novel's title pairs 'fantastic' with a word for a nimble dance step, from Milton's 'trip it as you go

explanation.surface: A question about what kind of fantasy Pratchett wrote.
explanation.walkthrough: Pratchett's 1986 Discworld novel borrows the stock phrase for dancing, from Milton's 'L'Allegro'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word missing from Pratchett's title completes the idiom for nimble dancing, 'trip the ___ fantastic'.

clue.text: Imogen's helper for whom piano is out of tune

indicators.note: an instrument out of tune has its notes jumbled, so the letters of piano is are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean servant whose piano is badly tuned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of tune' rearranges PIANO IS. In Cymbeline, Imogen's loyal servant refuses to kill her and helps her escape disguised as a boy.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cymbeline, Posthumus's servant disobeys orders to murder Imogen and instead aids her flight to Milford Haven.

clue.text: Choose artist to demonstrate what's complex

parts.note: to elect is to choose by vote
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist

explanation.surface: Picking a painter to show off something complicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what's complex' is cryptic: a Freudian Electra complex, a daughter's attachment to her father, is named after this figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Jung named the daughter-father complex after the Greek heroine who avenged her father Agamemnon.

clue.text: Georgia doctor gets a sort of old cello ()

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: A doctor from Georgia acquires an antique stringed instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: The viola da gamba, held between the knees, is the cello's Renaissance forerunner.
explanation.definitionFit: The viola da gamba, or leg-viol, is a bowed bass instrument predating the modern cello.

clue.text: Elinor was the one who represented sense

definitions.text: Elinor was the one who represented sense

parts.words: Elinor was the one who represented sense
parts.note: in Austen's novel the elder sister stands for sense and the younger, Marianne, for sensibility; the family surname is wanted

explanation.surface: A remark about which sister in a novel was the sensible one.
explanation.walkthrough: In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor embodies sense while her sister Marianne embodies sensibility; the clue wants their surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Elinor and Marianne belong to the family at the centre of Austen's Sense and Sensibility.

clue.text: Remarkable, like Thurber's O

definitions.meaning: James Thurber's 1957 fable is about pirates who ban the letter O, and its title gives it this adjective

explanation.surface: An extraordinary thing compared to a letter in a Thurber book.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means marvellous and also forms the title of Thurber's fable about a banned vowel.

clue.text: "… this holy lady / With cadence and subtle psalm" (W. H. Auden)

definitions.text: "… this holy lady / With cadence and subtle psalm" (W. H. Auden)

parts.words: "… this holy lady / With cadence and subtle psalm" (W. H. Auden)
parts.note: a quotation whose gap was lost in printing: an adjective meaning devout belongs between 'With' and 'cadence'

explanation.surface: Lines from Auden's anthem for St Cecilia's Day, on the saint's singing.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap was lost in printing: Auden's line runs 'With ___ cadence and subtle psalm', describing St Cecilia's song.
explanation.definitionFit: Auden describes the saint's music with an adjective meaning devout and deeply respectful.

clue.text: Cornish river employees for Sir John

parts.note: the Fal is a river in Cornwall flowing into Falmouth harbour
staff are employees

explanation.surface: Workers on a West Country river serve a knight.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fal is a river in Cornwall, in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's fat knight in the Henry IV plays and The Merry Wives of Windsor is Sir John.

clue.text: Lively music from the Hallé (growing livelier)

indicators.note: the answer is drawn out from within the letters of the orchestra's name and the word after

explanation.surface: Upbeat music played by a Manchester orchestra as it gets livelier.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hallé is a Manchester orchestra; the answer runs through halLÉ GROwing (accent ignored).
explanation.definitionFit: A brisk, lively tempo, and a movement played at it, is called by this Italian musical term.

clue.text: James, who was seduced by the music of chance

definitions.text: James, who was seduced by the music of chance

parts.words: James, who was seduced by the music of chance
parts.note: Paul Auster's novel The Music of Chance follows Jim, a fireman who gambles away an inheritance; his surname is wanted

explanation.surface: A man named James lured on by the thrill of gambling.
explanation.walkthrough: The protagonist of Paul Auster's novel The Music of Chance is Jim Nashe, drawn into a fateful poker game.
explanation.definitionFit: Auster's drifting ex-fireman hero bears this surname, shared with the Elizabethan writer Thomas.

clue.text: Churchyard cause of divine punishment for revolutionaries

definitions.text: Churchyard cause of divine punishment for revolutionaries

parts.words: Churchyard cause of divine punishment for revolutionaries
parts.note: Thomas Churchyard, the Elizabethan poet, wrote a tract titled for the whip of God's punishment on rebels in Ireland

explanation.surface: A graveyard as the source of heavenly retribution on rebels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Churchyard' is not a graveyard but the Elizabethan writer Thomas Churchyard, whose 1584 tract was The Scourge of Rebels.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a whip, and figuratively an agent of divine punishment, as in Churchyard's title.

clue.text: Spoke like Cicero, but classified zero

parts.note: zero is written as the round letter O
rated means graded or classified

explanation.surface: A Roman speaker given a score of nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Cicero was Rome's most famous public speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Cicero delivered formal speeches, and to deliver such a speech is to hold forth in public.

clue.text: Poet of Aurora Leigh

indicators.note: the answer is made of letters taken from inside the title Aurora Leigh

explanation.surface: Naming the author of Elizabeth Barrett Browning's verse novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The obvious answer is Barrett Browning, but she does not fit; the poet sits inside auRORA LEIGH. Sir Walter was an Elizabethan courtier-poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter, the Elizabethan courtier and explorer, also wrote poems such as 'The Nymph's Reply to the Shepherd'.

clue.text: Recalling Scott's moneylender, is a bill ()

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: Remembering a lender in a Walter Scott novel by an invoice.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scott's Ivanhoe, Isaac of York is the Jewish moneylender, father of Rebecca.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac of York lends money to knights in Scott's Ivanhoe.

clue.text: Arcadian city, for example, found in shrub ()

indicators.note: one piece is found inside another, so the abbreviation sits within the shrub

parts.note: the tea plant, Camellia sinensis, is an evergreen shrub
e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, 'for example'

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek town illustrated as lying within a bush.
explanation.definitionFit: Tegea was an ancient city-state in Arcadia, in the central Peloponnese.

clue.text: May it be with John Tanner, thought Shaw (4, )

definitions.text: May it be with John Tanner, thought Shaw

parts.words: May it be with John Tanner, thought Shaw
parts.note: plays on the blessing 'May the Force be with you': in Man and Superman, Shaw's hero Tanner is driven by the vital urge to reproduce

explanation.surface: A blessing a playwright bestows on his hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw's Man and Superman makes John Tanner the instrument of the evolutionary drive he named; the clue echoes 'May the Force be with you'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's term for the creative evolutionary urge that propels Tanner into marriage with Ann Whitefield.

clue.text: Gemini from radio's curious horoscope

indicators.note: the answer is taken from within the run of letters radio's curious

explanation.surface: Star signs read from an odd astrology slot on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: The twins sit inside raDIO'S CURIous; 'horoscope' only dresses the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Castor and Pollux, the heavenly twins of Greek myth, are the stars of the Gemini constellation.

clue.text: Consort seen with us in Gautier poem

indicators.note: the answer seen with the word us added makes the poem, so us is taken away from its title

parts.note: Albertus is Théophile Gautier's long narrative poem of 1832

explanation.surface: A royal husband appears alongside us in a French poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen with us' means the answer plus US gives Gautier's poem Albertus; Prince Albert was Queen Victoria's consort.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Albert was Queen Victoria's husband and so the royal consort.
